ABSTRACT
Monolithic perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-­junction solar cells have the potential to exceed the efficiency limits of per-
ovskite/silicon dual-­junction solar cells. However, the development of perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-­junction technology 
faces several significant hurdles, including the development and integration of a stable high bandgap perovskite absorber into 
the monolithic structure. Key issues include light-­induced halide segregation in mixed halide high bandgap perovskites and 
the risk of solvent damage to underlying layers during top-­cell deposition. To overcome these challenges, we developed a high 
bandgap, inorganic perovskite absorber, CsPbI2Br, using thermal evaporation at room temperature, eliminating the need for 
post-­deposition annealing. The resulting perovskite films exhibited a bandgap of 1.88 eV and demonstrated good photostability 
without any signs of halide segregation under continuous illumination probed over 3 h. Additionally, thermal evaporation offers a 
scalable approach for large-­scale production, further enhancing the potential for widespread adoption of this technology. This ad-
vancement enabled the incorporation of CsPbI2Br perovskite films into a monolithic perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-­junction 
device as the top-­cell absorber. Consequently, we developed the first triple-­junction device with an all-­inorganic perovskite top-­
cell absorber using the thermal evaporation technique, achieving an efficiency of 21%, with an open-­circuit voltage of 2.83 V over 
an active area of 1 cm2. The device underwent 100 h of fixed voltage measurement near maximum power point under ambient 
conditions without encapsulation. Remarkably, it not only withstood the measurement but also exhibited an improved efficiency 
of ~22% afterwards, further demonstrating the stability and reliability of our thermally evaporated CsPbI2Br perovskite absorber-­
based inorganic solar cell for monolithic triple-­junction perovskite/perovskite/silicon applications.

1   |   Introduction
The shift towards clean energy sources is paramount in mitigat-
ing the impending climate crisis. Multijunction solar cells hold 
great promise in this regard. They offer higher power conver-
sion efficiency (PCE) than single-­junction solar cells by stacking 
multiple light-­absorbing layers with complementary bandgaps 
to maximize absorption and minimize thermalization losses [1]. 
Among various design architectures of multijunction solar cells, 
the two-­terminal approach is likely the most relevant for the up-
coming market introduction, as it requires similar integration 
into a module as standard silicon photovoltaics. Cesium-­based 
lead halide inorganic perovskites are especially interesting for 
multijunction applications not only because of their high band-
gap but also due to their enhanced thermal stability as com-
pared to the organic–inorganic perovskite counterparts [2–4]. 
However, these all-­inorganic perovskites tend to suffer from 
phase stability issues, transitioning from the desired cubic per-
ovskite (or α-­perovskite) phase to orthorhombic perovskite (or 
δ-­perovskite) phase at room temperature [5, 6]. Substituting 
iodine atoms with bromine atoms in these perovskite lattices 
can stabilize the cubic perovskite phase and widens the band-
gap [2, 6]. CsPbI2Br is one of the most stable mixed-­halide inor-
ganic perovskite composition due to its optimal Goldschmidt's 
tolerance factor [7, 8]. Additionally, it offers a bandgap of ~1.9 eV 
[2, 7–9], which is suitable for top-­cell application in perovskite/
perovskite/silicon triple-­junction solar cells.
Although solution-­processed CsPbI2Br perovskites have been 
successfully utilized as high bandgap absorbers in all-­perovskite 
tandems [4, 10, 11], they have not yet been implemented into sil-
icon based multijunction solar cells. This is primarily due to the 
necessity of high annealing temperatures of ≥ 200°C [9, 12, 13] 
in solution processing techniques to achieve the appropriate 
α-­perovskite phase for these inorganic perovskites. Such high 
annealing temperatures can not only damage the underlying or-
ganic (common for charge transport layers) and perovskite layers 
but can also be detrimental for the bottom silicon heterojunction 
solar cell (SHJ), which has been the most common choice for 
multijunction applications [14]. At such high temperatures, hy-
drogen effuses out of the amorphous silicon (Si:H) layer degrad-
ing its passivation quality and hence the performance of SHJ 
cells [15]. It is worth noting that high annealing temperatures 
pose challenges for silicon-­based multijunction solar cells; they 
are less problematic in all-­perovskite tandems. This is because 
all-­perovskite multijunction cells use a superstrate configura-
tion, where the high bandgap perovskite is the first subcell to be 
fabricated on a glass substrate [16]. This design allows for high-­
temperature annealing without affecting the other layers. Some 
other bottlenecks associated with the solution-­processed tech-
niques are the issues related to process compatibility like upscal-
ing for industrial processes and damage to underlying layers due 
to solvent infiltration, especially when both the top and middle 
perovskite absorbers share similar solvent systems [17, 18]. To 
address these problems, we propose depositing CsPbI2Br per-
ovskite thin films using thermal evaporation. In this technique, 
precursor materials are evaporated in a high vacuum environ-
ment at controlled rates to produce thin films on the substrate, 
enabling conformal, large-­area deposition and eliminate the use 
of toxic solvents like DMF. This technique also avoids possible 
solvent penetration—and thus damage—towards the underlying 
middle cell. It also allows precise control over thin film param-
eters such as thickness and stoichiometry. Additionally, it is a 
well-­established industrial technique that offers opportunities 
for scalable manufacturing production lines. Till date, only a 
limited number of studies have explored vacuum deposition 
methods for CsPbI2Br perovskite thin films. Chen et  al. [19] 
used dual source coevaporation method, using CsBr and PbI2 
sources to deposit CsPbI2Br perovskite films. They optimized 
the annealing duration for the evaporated films to achieve a sta-
bilized efficiency of 11.5% for the inorganic perovskite absorber 
annealed at 260°C for 60 s. Later, the same group employed 
layer-­by-­layer vacuum deposition technique to deposit CsPbI2Br 
perovskite films. By altering the rates and the number of lay-
ers in the film stack, they reported an even higher efficiency 
of 13% for their single junction solar cell device using a similar 
annealing temperature of 260°C for the evaporated film stack 
[20]. Liao et al. [21] also used layer-­by-­layer (or sequential) evap-
oration technique, where they used an annealing temperature 
of 300°C to convert their 200-­nm CsBr and 312-­nm PbI2 layer 
stack to obtain the desired CsPbI2Br perovskite films. They also 
reported single junction solar cells in n-­i-­p configuration, show-
ing an overall efficiency of 9.96%. Gaonkar et al. [22] achieved 
an efficiency of 11.8% utilizing a similar sequential evaporation 
approach, however with alternating very thin layered stacks (4-­
nm CsBr and 6-­nm PbI2). They demonstrated stability at 200°C 
for 72 h, though still requiring an annealing temperature of 
200°C to convert their layered stack into perovskite film. Other 
sequential evaporation studies, such as Lee et al. [7], did also 
explore deposition sequences and stacking variations to deposit 
CsPbI2Br perovskite films, reporting an efficiency of ~11% for 
single junction cells but requiring a very high annealing tem-
perature of ~300°C to obtain the perovskite phase from the 
CsBr-­PbI2 layered stacks. Ma et al. [23] investigated the effect 
of rate ratios between CsBr and PbI2 sources on the coevapo-
ration deposited CsPbI2Br film properties and their stability. 
They found nonstoichiometric, CsBr-­rich perovskite films to be 
more stable than stoichiometric or PbI2-­rich perovskite films. 
However, the stoichiometric CsPbI2Br perovskite film gave bet-
ter solar cells efficiencies than the nonstoichiometric absorber, 
achieving a stabilized efficiency of 5.5% for the best perform-
ing solar cell in n-­i-­p configuration. Similarly, Park et al. [24] 
used coevaporation, achieving ~5.7% efficiency for CsPbI2Br 
absorber-­based n-­i-­p solar cell devices. Recently, Liu et al. [25] 
focused on the effects of humidity and postdeposition annealing 
on the optical properties and stability of coevaporated CsPbI2Br 
thin films, whereas Papadopoulou et  al. [26] used dynamic 
spectroscopic ellipsometry technique to study the effect of an-
nealing temperature on coevaporated CsPbI2Br perovskite film 
properties, emphasizing the importance of accounting for film 
roughness; for example, they linked tetragonal-­to-­cubic phase 
transition in the films to increased roughness. Beyond sequen-
tial and coevaporation methods, flash evaporation using single 
source has also been explored in literature as a faster alternative 
to deposit these inorganic perovskite thin films. It was first re-
ported for CsPbI2Br thin films by Tai et al. [27], where a laser 
was used as the heating source and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) 
as the evaporator. The CNTs coated with CsPbI2Br precursors 
in DMSO were scanned with a laser beam in a vacuum chamber 
to evaporate the perovskite precursor, which got deposited on 
the substrate within seconds. They also reported an efficiency 
of 9.4% for their single junction solar cell in n-­i-­p configuration

even greater for perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-­junction 
cells, as the perovskite middle-­cell having organic–inorganic

cannot withstand such high temperatures [29–32]. Thus, alter-
native low-­temperature processing strategies are necessary for 
integrating CsPbI2Br-­based top-­cell in silicon-­based multijunc-
tion architectures.
Igual-­Muñoz et  al. [3] previously demonstrated evaporation 
of CsPbI2Br films without annealing. However, this method 
has not yet been applied to fabricate multijunction solar cells. 
Additionally, light-­induced halide segregation remains a sig-
nificant challenge for mixed halide perovskite films with band-
gap higher than 1.65 eV [10, 33, 34], leading to voltage losses 
in related solar cell devices. Notably, the reports on thermally 
evaporated CsPbI2Br films have not yet addressed their photo-
stability. So far, limited efforts have been directed towards ad-
dressing these challenges in developing CsPbI2Br films; instead, 
high-­bandgap organic–inorganic perovskite films supported by 
various chemical additives and treatments have been promoted 
for application as the top-­cell absorber in triple-­junction devices 
[18, 35–38].
In this work, we addressed these challenges by optimizing the 
thermal evaporation process to produce good quality, photo-
stable CsPbI2Br thin films directly after evaporation, eliminat-
ing the need for postdeposition annealing. The as-­evaporated 
CsPbI2Br perovskite films not only displayed a high bandgap of 
1.88 eV but also showed good photostability, that is, no halide 
segregation under continuous illumination at 1-­Sun intensity 
in air for 3 h, without any additive engineering. We further re-

2   |   Results and Discussion
2.1   |   Evaporated Inorganic CsPbI2Br Perovskite 
Thin Films
To develop a low temperature deposition protocol for CsPbI2Br 
perovskite films, we optimized the thermal evaporation pro-
cess by using three precursor sources, namely, CsI, CsBr, and 
PbI2. Evaporation rate from the three sources was fine tuned 
to achieve a perovskite film with desired bandgap directly after 
the evaporation, while maintaining the substrate holder at room 
temperature. This adaptation was aimed at promoting halide 
alloying, allowing for the formation of the desired perovskite 
film without any temperature treatment. The deposition mecha-
nism of perovskite thin films using thermal evaporation differs 
significantly from solution processing techniques. In thermal 
evaporation, materials vaporize into a range of species, from 
intact molecules to dissociated molecules and atoms, which 
then condense on the substrate and react to form a solid film 
[39]. Evaporation conditions become particularly critical when 
working with materials featuring different vapor pressures; for 
instance, iodine compounds (CsI and PbI2) possess higher vapor 
pressures than their bromine counterparts (CsBr and PbBr2), 
causing them to vaporize more rapidly [39, 40]. Apart from 
evaporation rates, perovskite thin-­film properties like grain size 
are also closely related to process parameters such as base pres-
sure, substrate temperature, and the postdeposition annealing 
treatments [41, 42]. Figure 1a shows the schematic of the three-­
source evaporation process used in this study. The process pa-
rameters for the three-­source evaporation method are given in 
Section 4. In our study, we varied the evaporation rates of the 
three sources to obtain the desired perovskite film. Table S1 lists 
the various deposition rates tested for the three-­source evapora-
tion method along with the resulted perovskite film bandgaps. 
The changing bandgap as a function of the evaporation rates 
of the sources suggests a rearrangement in the film deposition 
during evaporation. Initially, we tested the conventional two-­
source coevaporation method using CsBr and PbI2 precursors; 
however, as reported in literature, the α-­perovskite phase for the 
dual-­source deposition technique was only obtained after sub-
jecting the evaporated films to a high annealing temperature of 
250°C [19, 23–26], making the technique unsuitable for mono-
lithic Si-­based multijunction solar cell applications. Details of 
the two-­source evaporation method are discussed in Figure S1.
Towards triple-­junction solar cell integration, we selected the 
perovskite films showing a bandgap of 1.88 eV, as estimated 
using the Tauc plot (Figure  1b,c) for this study. The desired 
bandgap was obtained using the evaporation rates of 0.8 Å/s 
for CsBr, 0.6 Å/s for PbI2, and 0.13 Å/s for CsI (see Table  S1). 
Figure  1d (inset) shows a photograph of the evaporated per-
ovskite film on a glass substrate, maintained at room tempera-
ture during deposition, which clearly exhibits a uniform brown

first fabricated semitransparent solar cells. To keep the design 
of single-­junction cells similar to the final triple-­junction cells, 
we fabricated our cells on ohmic Si substrates having flat front 
and rear side with 1-­cm2 active area. The CsPbI2Br perovskite 
absorber thickness was kept very thin, ~250 nm, and the cell 
was designed in a p-­i-­n configuration, similar to the top per-
ovskite subcell of a perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-­junction 
device (Figure  S5a). This reduced thickness, combined with 
a high bandgap, is necessary to achieve better current match-
ing between the perovskite top cell and the middle cell [43]. 
Evaporated Spiro-­TTB and C60 layers were used as the charge 
transport layers (CTLs) for hole and electron extraction, respec-
tively. Previous studies [44–46] have shown that the perovskite/
C60 interface is a primary source of voltage loss in the high 
bandgap perovskite solar cells, primarily due to high nonradi-
ative recombination losses and poor energy band alignment be-
tween the perovskite absorber and the C60 layer. To passivate 
the perovskite/C60 interface, 1 mg/mL F-­PEAI (fluoropheneth-
ylammonium iodide) in isopropanol (IPA) was used as depicted 
in Figure S5b. Apart from this passivation treatment, the rest 
of the device was entirely fabricated using the physical vapor

PL-­based iVOC imaging. Figure 3b shows the iVOC distribution

3   |   Conclusion
In summary, the paper addresses the key challenges in fabricat-
ing and applying a high bandgap inorganic perovskite film in 
perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-­junction solar cells. It pres-
ents the first successful integration of a thermally evaporated 
all-­inorganic CsPbI2Br perovskite top-­cell in a monolithic triple-­
junction solar cell. The developed perovskite demonstrated ex-
cellent photostability with no signs of halide segregation under 
continuous illumination for 3 h, leading to a stabilized PCE of 
21% for the triple-­junction solar cell. Although perovskite/per-
ovskite/silicon triple-­junction solar cells represent a complex 
and emerging technology, our work highlights promising solu-
tions for the robust processing of an efficient triple-­junction solar 
cell. Evaporation technique not only overcomes the challenges 
associated with solvent selection but also ensures uniform film 
deposition over large areas with better thickness control, a key 
factor that can be leveraged for further optimization and scal-
ing of the triple-­junction devices. The as developed monolithic 
perovskite/perovskite/silicon triple-­junction solar cell with 
thermally evaporated CsPbI2Br perovskite top cell not only en-
dured over 100 h of fixed voltage measurement under ambient 
conditions without encapsulation but also exhibited improved 
efficiency of ~22%. These results highlight the stability and re-
liability of these triple-­junction solar cells. Our future endeav-
ors will focus on improving the performance of the evaporated 
inorganic perovskite top cells by further optimizing the evapo-
ration process to enhance the device performance. This refine-
ment aims to enhance the crystallinity and bandgap of inorganic 
perovskite thin films at ambient temperature and optimize the 
selection of charge transport layers to further mitigate charge 
carrier selectivity losses. Additionally, for a truly scalable triple 
junction solar cell, it will be crucial to develop an evaporated 
middle cell and realize a fully evaporated perovskite/perovskite/
silicon triple junction.

4.1.3   |   Single Junction Solar Cells
The ohmic silicon substrates were first cleaned by spin coating 
200-­μL ethanol and then treated with UV-­ozone for 15 min, be-
fore being transferred to the glovebox for cell processing.
4.1.4   |   Perovskite Middle-­Cell (Eg ~ 1.56 eV)
A 120-­uL PTAA solution was spin coated at 6000 rpm for 30 s 
and annealed at 100°C for 10 min on a preheated hotplate. 
It was followed by spin coating 60-­μL PFN-­Br solution at 
5000 rpm for 20 s on top to improve the wetting for perovskite 
deposition. A 150-­μL perovskite solution was then spin 
coated at 4000 rpm for 35 s; after 10 s, 300-­μL ethyl acetate 
was dropped on the spinning substrates. Samples were now 
annealed at 100°C for 30 min. Samples were then transferred 
to a different glovebox for ETL deposition. Fifteen nanome-
ters of C60 was thermally evaporated with an evaporation rate 
of 0.2 Å/s. As a buffer layer to avoid sputter damage, 20-­nm 
SnOx layer was deposited by atomic layer deposition at 80 °C. 
Twenty-­five-­nanometer ITO was then DC sputtered as recom-
bination layer using a shadow mask defining an active area of 
1 cm2. The metallization was done by evaporating 200-­0nm 
silver, and finally, 100-­nm MgFx was evaporated as antireflec-
tion coating.
4.2   |   Perovskite Top-­Cell (Eg ~ 1.88 eV)
Eight nanometers of Spiro-­TTB was deposited with a nom-
inal evaporation rate of 0.2 Å/s at base pressure lower than 
3 × 10−6 Torr and a working pressure lower than 4 × 10–6 Torr. 
Afterwards, samples were transferred to a Lesker mini-­
Spectros system evaporator for perovskite deposition. For this 
purpose, precursor materials CsBr, PbI2, and CsI were loaded 
in ceramic crucibles for coevaporation in a Lesker mini-­
Spectros system (at a base pressure lower than 2 × 10–6 Torr 
and a working pressure lower than 3 × 10−6 Torr). The rates 
as measured by quartz crystal monitors for the CsBr, PbI2, 
and CsI sources were maintained at 0.8, 0.6, and 0.13 Å/s, re-
spectively, to obtain the CsPbI2Br perovskite thin films with 
a bandgap of 1.88 eV and a thickness of ~250 nm. The evap-
oration temperature was ~460°C for CsBr, ~300°C for PbI2, 
and ~420°C for CsI. Ceramic crucibles, made of alumina 
(Al2O3), were used for evaporation. For passivation with F-­
PEAI, the procedure shown in the Supporting Information 
text (Figure  S5b) was followed. The samples were annealed 
at 100°C for 15 min prior to passivation. Annealed samples 
were then spin coated with 150 μL of F-­PEAI solution in IPA 
at 4000 rpm for 40 s. The F-­PEAI coated samples were sub-
sequently annealed at 100°C for 5 min. The substrate holder 
was maintained at 25°C. The procedure for rest of the layers, 
including C60, SnOx, ITO, Ag, and MgFx, remained the same 
as described above.
4.2.1   |   Triple-­Junction Solar Cells
The triple-­junction solar cell was silicon heterojunction 
(SHJ) solar cell with flat front and rear-­side textured as the 
bottom cell. The procedure for fabricating the SHJ bottom 
cells can be found in our previous publications [58, 59]. A 
25-­nm-­thick ITO layer acts as the recombination layer be-
tween the bottom cell and the perovskite middle cell. The 
middle-­cell fabrication procedure is like the single-­junction 
solar cell fabrication as mentioned above. A 15-­nm-­thick ITO 
layer was sputtered as the recombination layer between the 
perovskite subcells. Inorganic perovskite-­based top cell was 
then deposited on the samples according to the procedure 
mentioned above.
A shadow mask was used for all three ITO layers deposition 
defining 1-­cm2 active cell area. The thicknesses of the recom-
bination layers used between subcells were optimized in our 
previous publication [17].

pared by dissolving appropriate stoichiometric amounts of FAI, 
MABr and CsI, PbBr 2, and PbI 2 with 1% Pb excess in solvent 
mixture of DMF:DMSO (4:1) and stirred overnight.
For preparation of PTAA (3 mg/mL) and PFN-  Br (0.5 mg/mL) 
solutions, powders were dissolved in toluene and methanol, re -
spectively, and stirred overnight.
4.1.3   |   Single Junction Solar Cells
The ohmic silicon substrates were first cleaned by spin coating 
200- μL ethanol and then treated with UV-  ozone for 15 min, be-
fore being transferred to the glovebox for cell processing.
4.1.4   |   Perovskite Middle- Cell (Eg ~ 1.56 eV)
A 120- uL PTAA solution was spin coated at 6000 rpm for 30 s 
and annealed at 100°C for 10 min on a preheated hotplate. 
It was followed by spin coating 60-  μL PFN-  Br solution at 
5000 rpm for 20 s on top to improve the wetting for perovskite 
deposition. A 150-  μL perovskite solution was then spin 
coated at 4000 rpm for 35 s; after 10 s, 300-  μL ethyl acetate 
was dropped on the spinning substrates. Samples were now 
annealed at 100°C for 30 min. Samples were then transferred 
to a different glovebox for ETL deposition. Fifteen nanome -
ters of C60 was thermally evaporated with an evaporation rate 
of 0.2 Å/s. As a buffer layer to avoid sputter damage, 20-  nm 
SnOx layer was deposited by atomic layer deposition at 80 °C. 
Twenty- five- nanometer ITO was then DC sputtered as recom-
bination layer using a shadow mask defining an active area of 
1 cm2. The metallization was done by evaporating 200-  0nm 
silver, and finally, 100- nm MgFx was evaporated as antireflec-
tion coating.
4.2   |   Perovskite Top- Cell (Eg ~ 1.88 eV)
Eight nanometers of Spiro-  TTB was deposited with a nom -
inal evaporation rate of 0.2 Å/s at base pressure lower than 
3 × 10−6 Torr and a working pressure lower than 4 × 10–6 Torr. 
Afterwards, samples were transferred to a Lesker mini-  
Spectros system evaporator for perovskite deposition. For this 
purpose, precursor materials CsBr, PbI2, and CsI were loaded 
in ceramic crucibles for coevaporation in a Lesker mini-  
Spectros system (at a base pressure lower than 2 × 10–6 Torr 
and a working pressure lower than 3 × 10−6 Torr). The rates 
as measured by quartz crystal monitors for the CsBr, PbI 2, 
and CsI sources were maintained at 0.8, 0.6, and 0.13 Å/s, re-
spectively, to obtain the CsPbI 2Br perovskite thin films with 
a bandgap of 1.88 eV and a thickness of ~250 nm. The evap -
oration temperature was ~460°C for CsBr, ~300°C for PbI 2, 
and ~420°C for CsI. Ceramic crucibles, made of alumina 
(Al2O3), were used for evaporation. For passivation with F-  
PEAI, the procedure shown in the Supporting Information  
text (Figure  S5b) was followed. The samples were annealed 
at 100°C for 15 min prior to passivation. Annealed samples 
were then spin coated with 150 μL of F- PEAI solution in IPA 
at 4000 rpm for 40 s. The F- PEAI coated samples were sub -
sequently annealed at 100°C for 5 min. The substrate holder 
was maintained at 25°C. The procedure for rest of the layers, 
including C60, SnOx, ITO, Ag, and MgF x, remained the same 
as described above.
4.2.1   |   Triple- Junction Solar Cells
The triple-  junction solar cell was silicon heterojunction 
(SHJ) solar cell with flat front and rear-  side textured as the 
bottom cell. The procedure for fabricating the SHJ bottom 
cells can be found in our previous publications [ 58, 59 ]. A 
25- nm- thick ITO layer acts as the recombination layer be -
tween the bottom cell and the perovskite middle cell. The 
middle- cell fabrication procedure is like the single-  junction 
solar cell fabrication as mentioned above. A 15-  nm- thick ITO 
layer was sputtered as the recombination layer between the 
perovskite subcells. Inorganic perovskite-  based top cell was 
then deposited on the samples according to the procedure 
mentioned above.
A shadow mask was used for all three ITO layers deposition 
defining 1- cm2 active cell area. The thicknesses of the recom -
bination layers used between subcells were optimized in our 
previous publication [17].

4.3.1   |   EQE and I–V Measurements
The EQE and spectral response were measured using an 
in- house measurement setup. The measurements of triple-  
junction solar cells are performed according to [60, 61]. For the 
measurements of the top cell, red and infrared (IR) light emit-
ting diodes (LEDs) were used. For measurements of middle-  
cell blue and IR LEDs, and for the silicon bottom cell, blue and 
red LEDs were illuminated on the triple-  junction device. In

The spectral responses (SR) of the subcells were then used to 
calculate the spectra of solar simulator according to the pro-
cedure described in [62]. This ensures that the spectrum is

subcell under the simulator spectrum matches that under the 
AM1.5g spectrum. A Wavelabs SINUS 220 LED-­based solar 
simulator containing 20 different LEDs was used for I–V mea-
surements. I–V curves were then measured with a voltage 
sweep up to 1200 mV for single-­junction solar cells and up to 
2900 mV for triple-­junction solar cells, using a voltage step of 
6 mV and a scan rate of 60 mV/s.
4.4   |   PL Intensity
4.4.1   |   X-­Ray Diffraction (XRD) Measurements
X-­ray diffractograms were recorded using a Bruker D8 
Advance tool with Cu Kα source. Measurements were carried 
out in step size of 0.01°, and time per step was set at 0.5 s. The 
gracing incidence XRD was recorded at an angle of incidence 
of 5°.
4.4.2   |   SEM Measurements
Film morphology and cross-­section at different magnifications 
were obtained using a Schottky emission SEM (Zeiss, Auriga 60) 
at 5 kV.
4.4.3   |   PL Measurements
LuQY Pro Radiative efficiency meter model LP20-­32 instrument 
was used for PL and the implied open-­circuit voltage measure-
ments. The laser wavelength of 532 nm and spot size of 0.1 cm2 
were used to excite the perovskite samples at one sun equivalent 
intensity for this purpose.
4.4.4   |   Hyperspectral Imaging
Steady-­state PL measurements were performed using a 
hyperspectral luminescence imaging system, which includes 
an optical microscope with a 100X objective and a 405-­nm 
laser at 1-­Sun equivalent intensity. Each scan took approxi-
mately 2 min. All samples were nonencapsulated and mea-
sured in air.
4.4.5   |   PL-­Based iVOC Imaging
A measurement system developed at Fraunhofer ISE and built by 
Intego GmbH was used for the acquisition of PL images. A 450-­
nm laser was used to homogeneously illuminate the samples at 
1-­Sun equivalent intensity. A 730-­nm LED was used to subcell 
selectively illuminate the middle cell in the triple-­junction de-
vice in Figure S14. More details on the measurement system and 
the iVOC imaging method can be found here [63].
4.4.6   |   Microscopic PL Measurements
A commercially available confocal Raman scanning microscope 
(Witec) was used to focus a laser beam (355 nm) for the 2D per-
ovskite measurements. The laser spot size was approximately 
1 μm for the used objective lens with 20X magnification. The 
emitted PL signal was spectrally resolved by coupling it via a 
dichroic mirror to a Czerny–Turner-­type spectrometer and de-
tecting the signal with a silicon charge-­coupled device (CCD) 
linear array detector.
4.4.7   |   UV–Vis Measurements
Reflectance and transmittance data in the wavelength range of 
300–1200 nm were collected using a lambda 950 spectrometer 
(PerkinElmer) tool. Absorptance for the perovskite films was 
estimated using the formula A = 1−R−T.
4.4.8   |   Transient PL Measurements
TrPLs were performed with a hybrid photomultiplier detector 
assembly from Picoquant and a time-­correlated single photon 
counting digitizer (Timeharp). A 515-­nm laser (Omicron) was 
used as a light source, and it was modulated digitally with a trig-
ger signal generated by an arbitrary wave-­form generator. The 
incident intensity was set to 51 mW/cm2. The on-­time was set to 
500 ns, and the off-­time to 1.5 μs. The integration time was set 
to 300 s.
4.4.9   |   X-­Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy 
Measurements
XPS spectra were acquired on a SPECS Surface Nano Analysis 
GmbH, EnviroESCA X-­ray photoelectron spectrometer 
(PHOIBOS 150 NAP analyzer, 1D Delay Line Detector, mono-
chromatic Al Kα radiation at 1486.6 eV, incident angle 55°). 
Survey spectra were obtained with a pass energy of 100 eV, 
high-­resolution spectra with 50 eV, and 20 accumulative 
scans. The signal of the I 3d5/2 electrons was used as binding 
energy reference at 618.50 eV. No charge control was required; 
the C 1s signals vary in the range of 284.2 and 284.3 eV. A 
depth profile was generated using an GCIB 10S ion gun from 
Ionoptika (10 kV, Ar+ ion sputtering, 6 × 6 mm2). The expected 
decomposition of perovskites, the occurrence of Pb(0) due to 
X-­ray exposure and sputtering, was observed as reported in 
literature [48, 64, 65]. Therefore, a low sputter rate was chosen 
for gentle etching. The sputter limits were set to 720-­s etch-
ing time. The semiquantitative analysis was done considering 
temperature, mean free pathway, and the usage of relative 
sensitivity factors from CasaXPS. The elemental ratios were 
then calculated from the elemental distribution of the semi-
quantitative analysis.
